title: The Fear Doesn't Go Away at the Top. It Just Costs More.
author: Lead with Kelly
summary: In this personal leadership essay, the author describes preparing an honest status update for a CEO — one that accurately named the problems and what should have been done differently — only to have a senior leader rewrite it before the meeting to hide difficult truths. What followed was a revelation: the fear that drove the rewrite wasn't unique to one man. It ran through every level of the organization, with each person sanding down the truth before passing it upward so the person above them would never have to confront the uncomfortable thing. The CEO at the top, far from being free, was the most fearful of all: so shielded from honest feedback for years that he had no practice absorbing challenge. The author concludes that hierarchies are never really managed from the top — everyone answers to someone above them, all the way up to a market that answers to no one. The only escape is to build something of your own where the honest deck doesn't get rewritten.
points: Senior leaders who are rarely challenged lose the capacity to absorb hard truths — and when pressure finally arrives from the market, the fear travels down through every organizational level.

When every level in a hierarchy is managing the impression of the level above it, no one is actually steering: decisions stop being about what is right and start being about what the next person up needs to see.

The 'top' is an illusion of freedom — the director answers to the VP, the VP to the CEO, the CEO to the board, and the board to the market; the market answers to no one, so no one in the chain is ever free.
A company can look like it is being managed when it is really just a long chain of people flinching in the same direction, with the story protected over the substance whenever both can't win.
The only way out of the hierarchy of fear is to build something where you own the honest version of the work and no one above you can rewrite it to protect someone else's comfort.
quotes: It was not that he thought I was wrong. He knew I was right. That was the problem.
He became a boy chasing a gold star. He wanted permission for everything.
A whole company, busy hiding the same fact from each other, one rung at a time.
The director answers to the VP, the VP to the CEO, the CEO to the board, and the board to the market. And the market answers to no one, which is exactly why no one in the whole chain is ever free.
When every level is managing the level above it, nobody is really steering.
A company that looks like it is being run is sometimes just a very long chain of people flinching.
The substance is just what you would have done if no one were watching. And someone is always watching.
